text: A dataset consists of many vectors with the same number of components. This section combines them into a single table of numbers, a matrix, and establishes how to write and calculate with matrices. Matrices The table of apartments is more than four separate vectors it is one object that you want to calculate with as a whole. A grayscale image is also a table, namely of brightness values, arranged in rows and columns. Such a rectangular array of numbers is called a matrix. A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of real numbers in rows and columns The number in row and column is called an entry of the matrix. The pair is called the size of the matrix. Matrices are written in bold capital letters, their entries with the corresponding lowercase letter and two indices first the row, then the column. The th column of is a vector with components; it is called . The matrix is then also written as a row of its columns, . A vector with components is a matrix of size , and a row with numbers is a matrix of size . Two matrices are equal if they have the same size and the same entry in every position. Matrices of the same size are added and multiplied by a number entry by entry, just like vectors and . The matrix has size , the entries and , and the second column . A grayscale image of pixels that shows a bright cross on a dark background is the matrix with the rows , and . Furthermore, ⁠ In short A matrix is a rectangular table of numbers with rows and columns; the entry is in row and column . If you read out an image row by row and string the rows together, the matrix becomes a long vector the cross becomes the vector , and a image becomes a vector in . The numbers stay the same, but one piece of information is lost in this notation which pixels are neighbors. The pixel directly below another one is positions further back in the long vector. For calculations that weight each feature individually, this does not matter. For calculations that want to exploit neighborhoods, the matrix form is the more natural one. Square matrices and diagonal matrices Some matrices occur so often that they have their own names. In all three cases the shape of the table is particularly simple. A matrix with the same number of rows and columns is called square . The entries of a square matrix form its diagonal , which runs from the top left to the bottom right. A square matrix whose entries off the diagonal are all zero is called a diagonal matrix . For a vector , is the diagonal matrix with the diagonal entries . The matrix whose entries are all zero is called the zero matrix and is written . The second matrix has a diagonal entry zero and is still a diagonal matrix; the only requirement is that all entries off the diagonal are zero. Instead of you write for short. ⁠ In short A square matrix has as many rows as columns; a diagonal matrix has nonzero entries only on the diagonal. The data matrix The apartment table from Subsection 1.2 vektoren daten als zahlenlisten.html stufe 1 2 is a matrix four rows, one per apartment, and three columns, one per feature. This arrangement, one example per row, is the standard form of a dataset Fig. 27 abb 27 . The data matrix of the apartment dataset. Each row is an example, the vector written as a row blue apartment 2 . Each column is the feature column of one feature across all examples orange the floor areas . The entry belongs to both. For a dataset with the examples , the data matrix is the matrix whose row is the example , written as a row The entry is the value of feature for example , exactly as agreed in Subsection 1.3 vektoren daten als zahlenlisten.html stufe 1 3 . Column of is the feature column of feature from Subsection 4.3 abstande und einheiten.html stufe 4 3 all values of this feature across all examples. So the rows belong to the examples and the columns to the features. Component of the mean of the examples is the mean of column . For the apartment dataset, The entry is the number of rooms of apartment 3, the first column contains all floor areas, and its mean is the first component of . ⁠ In short The data matrix contains one example per row and one feature per column. This series writes the examples as rows, as in a spreadsheet and in most current textbooks and software libraries. Some texts do it the other way around and place the examples side by side as columns; their data matrix then has size . The letters vary as well often the number of examples is called and the number of features , and example number is written , with the index at the top in parentheses. The content does not change. So when you read someone else's text, first check what is a row and what is a column there. What is the size of ? Give , and the third column of . Set up the data matrix of the three texts from Subsection 5.4 winkel und ahnlichkeit.html stufe 5 4 . What do , and the entry mean? A grayscale image of pixels shows a bright “L” the first column and the bottom row are bright , everything else is dark . Write down the matrix and read it out row by row into a vector. How many components does it have? a has size . We have row 1, column 3 and row 2, column 1 ; the third column is . b with texts and words. The entry says the third word, “election”, does not occur in the second text. c The matrix has the rows , , and . Read out row by row, it gives the vector with components.

text: So far the input was given and the output was sought. This section asks the reverse question which input produces a given output? That is a system of linear equations. The section shows how to solve it and when it has no solution, exactly one solution or infinitely many solutions. Systems of equations in matrix form From school you know problems like this two numbers and satisfy and ; what are they? The left hand sides are the components of a matrix–vector product. So the problem asks which vector is mapped by the matrix to ? For a matrix and a vector , is called a system of linear equations with equations and the unknowns . The matrix is called the coefficient matrix , the vector the right hand side . Every vector that satisfies 12.1 gl 12 1 is called a solution . Written out, row contains the equation . The system has the solution and . The coefficient matrix is familiar from Subsection 11.2 einheitsmatrix und inverse.html stufe 11 2 , with the inverse . If you multiply the system by this inverse from the left, the solution appears immediately . ⁠ In short A system of linear equations asks which input produces the output . Row picture and column picture As with the matrix–vector product, there are two ways to read a system of equations. Row picture. Each equation on its own describes a set of points. With two unknowns, is a line in the plane, and so is . A solution must satisfy both equations, that is, lie on both lines it is their point of intersection Fig. 38 abb 38 , left . With three unknowns, each equation is a plane in space. Column picture. By the column view 7.3 das matrix vektor produkt.html gl 7 3 , . The column picture immediately answers when there is a solution at all. The vectors form the column space Subsection 7.4 das matrix vektor produkt.html stufe 7 4 . The system is solvable for , for instance with , but not for by Subsection 7.4 das matrix vektor produkt.html stufe 7 4 , the column space is only the line in the direction of . ⁠ In short In the row picture, a solution is a point common to all equations; in the column picture, it is the choice of coefficients with which the columns give the right hand side. Gaussian elimination With two unknowns you can find the solution by inspection. With three or more you need a method that always works. The idea is the same as in school you subtract a multiple of one equation from another so that an unknown disappears. You repeat this until the last equation contains only one unknown. For this you write down only the numbers the coefficient matrix and, separated by a vertical bar, the right hand side. This table is called the augmented matrix . Gaussian elimination transforms the augmented matrix with three row operations add a multiple of one row to another row; swap two rows; multiply a row by a nonzero number. The goal is row echelon form in each row, the first nonzero entry is preceded by at least one more zero than in the row above. Then you determine the unknowns from the bottom up back substitution . A system and the system obtained from it by row operations have the same solutions. Every solution of the old system also satisfies the new equations, because these are sums and multiples of the old ones. But each of the three operations can also be undone subtract the multiple again, swap the rows back, divide by the number. So, conversely, every solution of the new system also satisfies the old one. The system If you subtract the first row twice from the second and once from the third, disappears from both. The solution is , and substituting it into all three equations confirms it. ⁠ In short Gaussian elimination eliminates the unknowns step by step with row operations, which do not change the solutions, and then substitutes from the bottom up. If is invertible, the solution is . This is useful for reasoning but unfavorable as a way of computing. For a system with equations and unknowns, Gaussian elimination needs about basic arithmetic operations; computing the inverse costs about , three times as much, and the product comes on top of that. Moreover, a computer calculates with finitely many digits. The inverse can then only be represented in rounded form, and direct elimination usually gives more accurate results. So the inverse is above all a tool for thinking and deriving, not for computing. This section measures how many truly different directions a matrix contains, and it shows what it means for data when features carry the same information twice. The span The column space of a matrix is the set of all linear combinations of its columns. The same construction gives a set for every list of vectors, and this set gets its own name Fig. 39 abb 39 . The span of the vectors is the set of all their linear combinations So the column space of a matrix is the span of its columns. Along with any two of its vectors, every linear combination of them also lies in the span; adding and taking multiples never lead you out of it. is the line of all multiples . Linear independence In Fig. 39 abb 39 b , the second vector brings nothing new it already lies in the span of the first. A dataset can have the same weakness. If it contains the number of bedrooms, the number of living rooms and the total number of rooms, the third column is the sum of the first two and carries no information of its own. You need a word for the property that nothing in a list of vectors is superfluous. Vectors are called linearly independent if holds only for . Otherwise they are called linearly dependent . Equivalently, linearly dependent means at least one of the vectors is a linear combination of the others. Indeed, if 13.2 gl 13 2 holds with a coefficient , you can solve for . Basis and dimension If you want to describe a span as economically as possible, you take as few vectors as necessary, but enough to reach everything. Such a list is like a coordinate system every vector of the span then has exactly one representation in terms of it. A list of linearly independent vectors whose span is a set is called a basis of . The number of vectors in a basis is called the dimension of , written . A set has many different bases, but they all consist of the same number of vectors; this is a theorem of linear algebra on which the definition of dimension rests. The unit vectors form a basis of , the standard basis ; that is why . If is a basis of , then every vector has exactly one representation . The line has dimension , even though its vectors have two components. ⁠ In short A basis is a list of independent vectors that spans everything; its length is the dimension. The rank of a matrix A matrix with columns can contain fewer than truly different directions. The number of directions that remain when you leave out everything superfluous tells you how much a matrix actually accomplishes. The rank of a matrix is the largest number of linearly independent columns of . It equals the dimension of its column space. The largest number of linearly independent columns of a matrix equals the largest number of linearly independent rows. In particular, for . If , then has full rank . In practice, you determine the rank with Gaussian elimination row operations do not change it, and in row echelon form it is the number of rows that do not consist entirely of zeros. has rank the second column is twice the first, and likewise the second row is twice the first. For you subtract the first and the second row from the third and get the rows , , . Two rows are nonzero, so ; indeed, the third column is the sum of the first two. The data matrix of the apartments has full rank . ⁠ In short The rank counts how many truly different directions the columns of a matrix contain, and there are just as many as in its rows. This is not obvious the rows and the columns of a matrix live in completely different spaces. A short argument goes like this. Suppose columns of are linearly independent and every other column is a linear combination of them. These columns form a matrix . Each column of is then times a coefficient vector with components. So the rows have at most as many independent directions as the columns. Applying the same argument to , whose columns are the rows of , gives the reverse inequality. So the two numbers are equal. The null space and the rank–nullity theorem A matrix with columns accepts vectors from directions. Some of these directions arrive in the result; the rest are mapped to the zero vector and are lost. The lost directions form a set of their own. text: A linear map deforms the grid of the plane, and in the process areas become larger or smaller. This section determines the factor by which they change. This factor is a single number, the determinant, and it also tells you whether a matrix is invertible. The determinant of a matrix The unit square has area . A matrix maps it to the parallelogram spanned by its two columns Subsection 8.3 lineare abbildungen.html stufe 8 3 . How large is the area of this parallelogram? Figure 40 abb 40 shows it for . Left the unit square with area ; right its image under , the parallelogram formed by the columns and . It has area . Dashed the enclosing rectangle, from which the area can be computed. Let the columns be and with all four numbers positive, and let lie above and to the left of , as in Fig. 40 abb 40 . The parallelogram with the corners , , , fits into the rectangle with sides and . To leave only the parallelogram, you cut out of the rectangle two triangles with legs and , two triangles with legs and , and two rectangles with sides and For . The determinant of the matrix is the number Its absolute value is the area of the parallelogram spanned by the columns, that is, the factor by which changes the area of the unit square. It is the same number that appears in the denominator of the inverse 11.2 einheitsmatrix und inverse.html gl 11 2 . , , and . The stretch changes the shape of the square but not its area what it gains in width, it loses in height. ⁠ In short In absolute value, the determinant of a matrix is the factor by which the map changes the area of the unit square. The sign of the determinant An area is never negative, but the determinant can be. Its sign carries additional information whether the map reflects the plane. In the unit square, lies counterclockwise from . If this stays so for the images, that is, if also lies counterclockwise from , then . If lies clockwise from , the plane has been reflected, and . This property is called orientation a positive determinant preserves the orientation, a negative one reverses it. The reflection across the axis, , has determinant the area stays the same, the orientation is reversed. If you swap the columns of a matrix, the determinant changes its sign . The rotation by has , the shear , and the flattening has determinant . ⁠ In short The absolute value of the determinant is the area factor; its sign tells whether the map reflects. The area factor holds for every figure So far we have looked at the unit square. But a linear map treats every location in the plane in the same way, and therefore it changes the area of every figure by the same factor. If maps a figure of area , the image has area . Lay a fine grid of small squares with side length over the figure. A square with the corner has the corners , , and . Its image has the corners , , and it is the parallelogram formed by and , shifted to . Its area is , no matter where the square was. So every small square becomes larger or smaller by the same factor . The figure consists approximately of such squares, and the finer the grid, the more accurate the approximation. Therefore the factor holds for the whole figure. The disk of radius has area . The stretch turns it into an ellipse with semi axes and . The area of the ellipse is , that is, exactly times the area of the disk. The triangle with the corners , , has area ; under it becomes the triangle with the corners , , and area . ⁠ In short A linear map changes the area of every figure by the same factor , because it treats every small cell of the grid in the same way. Determinants of larger matrices In space, the unit cube becomes the parallelepiped spanned by the three columns of the matrix, a slanted box. Its volume is the factor by which the map changes volumes. For larger matrices, too, there is such a number. You compute it by reducing it to determinants of smaller matrices. For , . If you apply two maps one after the other, the first changes the volume by its factor, and the second changes the result once more by its own factor. The factors multiply. text: Not every calculation with vectors and matrices is a matrix product. This section presents the calculations that work entry by entry, and it extends vectors and matrices to arrays of numbers with more than two indices, as they are needed for images. The Hadamard product A shopkeeper has the list of quantities sold and the list of unit prices. For each item he wants the revenue, that is, quantity times price, but not yet the sum. This is a product entry by entry. For two vectors or two matrices of the same size, the Hadamard product is the product entry by entry The Hadamard product is not the matrix product. The matrix product forms dot products of rows and columns; the Hadamard product only multiplies entries in the same position. Two connections with things you already know if you add up the Hadamard product of two vectors, you get their dot product, . And the Hadamard product with a fixed vector is multiplication by a diagonal matrix . , and is the dot product. For matrices, With a vector of zeros and ones you can mask out features drops the number of rooms of apartment 1. ⁠ In short The Hadamard product multiplies entry by entry; it is not the matrix product. Elementwise functions Often you apply the same function to every entry of a vector you square all errors, take the absolute value of all of them or round all values. For a function and a vector , applied elementwise is the vector . For matrices, the same is done entry by entry. Many norms can be written this way the 1 norm is the sum of the elementwise absolute values, , and the square of the Euclidean norm is the sum of the elementwise squares. An elementwise function is in general not linear elementwise squaring turns into the vector with the entries , not . The real estate agent's error vector was . The elementwise absolute values give with the sum , the 1 norm. For appraiser A from Subsection 3.5 normen die groe eines vektors.html stufe 3 5 , the elementwise squares give with the sum . ⁠ In short An elementwise function acts on each entry separately; in general it is not linear. Adding a vector to every row To center a whole dataset, you subtract the same vector, the mean of the examples, from every row of the data matrix. In the same way, the affine prediction adds the same intercept to every component. Such calculations need a notation. The mean of the examples is given by a matrix–vector product , because its component is , the mean of column . The matrix whose rows all equal is the outer product . So the centered data matrix is and its row is the vector . Many texts write for short and mean by it subtract the row vector from every row. Strictly speaking, the difference of an matrix and a matrix is not defined; the shorthand always stands for 15.2 gl 15 2 . For the apartments, and Each column is the centered feature column from Subsection 4.3 abstande und einheiten.html stufe 4 3 and sums to zero. ⁠ In short Adding a vector to every row of a matrix means forming ; the common shorthand means exactly this. Tensors A scalar is a single number, a vector a list with one index, a matrix a table with two indices. A color image needs three row, column and color channel. A stack of color images needs four. All these arrays of numbers are gathered under one name. In machine learning, a tensor is an array of numbers whose entries are numbered by indices. Each index runs along an axis . The list of the axis lengths is called the shape of the tensor. A scalar is a tensor with axes, a vector in one with a single axis of length , a matrix in one with the shape . A tensor of shape has entries. Figure 42 abb 42 shows the first few levels. Tensors with to axes a scalar, a vector with entries, a matrix such as a grayscale image , a color image made of three channels for red, green and blue, and a stack of such color images indicated by three images . A color image with pixels and three color channels is a tensor of shape with entries. The entry with the indices is the brightness of the first channel, that is, red, at the pixel in row and column . ⁠ In short A tensor is an array of numbers with any number of axes; scalar, vector and matrix are the cases with , and axes. In physics, a tensor is more than an array of numbers, for example the inertia tensor, which states how hard it is to rotate a body about each axis, or the tensor that describes how strongly a loaded beam is pulled or pushed in each direction. There, a tensor comes with a rule for how its entries change when you rotate the coordinate system; the entries alone do not make it a tensor. In machine learning this rule is absent there, a tensor is just a multidimensional array of numbers. The word is the same, the concept is a different one. text: What this is about In Chapter 1 /wissen/en/informatik/machine learning/mathematische grundlagen/vektoren und matrizen/vektoren und matrizen.html one question was left open. Four apartments are described by their floor area and their number of rooms, and their prices are known. We are looking for two weights with which the weighted sum hits every price. Such weights do not exist four equations in two unknowns contradict one another. With measured data this is almost always the case. You have more measurements than unknowns, every measurement is slightly inaccurate, and the system of equations has no solution. Still, you need weights, namely the ones that are off by as little as possible. This chapter pursues this question and two more that turn out to be closely related. Are there directions in which a matrix only makes an arrow longer or shorter without rotating it, and what do these directions reveal about the matrix? And can every matrix be split into a few simple building blocks, ordered by importance, so that the unimportant ones can be left out? On top of that comes a practical question how much does the result of a calculation change when the data are slightly wrong? The payoff with the answers, you fit a line or another simple rule to measured values so that the error is as small as possible. You can tell whether a function of several variables has a hollow, a ridge or a saddle. You approximate an image or a large table with a few numbers and know how much is lost in the process. And you can judge whether a computed result can be trusted. The tools of this chapter show up in almost all later parts of the series. How to work with this chapter. The sections build on each other, and every new term has its own subsection with an example. Expandable boxes contain background why a method works and where it comes from , derivations and proofs; you do not need them to read on. This section finds these directions and the stretch factors that belong to them. They are the natural axes of a matrix. What you need for this complex numbers The search for stretch factors leads to polynomial equations, and not every one of them has real solutions. text: What this is about A number often depends on many other numbers. The price that the weighted sum from Chapter 1 /wissen/en/informatik/machine learning/mathematische grundlagen/vektoren und matrizen/vektoren und matrizen.html predicts for an apartment depends on every weight and every feature. The length of an error vector depends on each of its components. The result of a long calculation depends on every value it starts with. This chapter asks how strongly and in which direction does such a number change if you change one of its inputs a little? And if there are thousands of inputs in which direction must you shift all of them at once so that the number grows fastest or falls fastest? On top of that comes a practical question. Often the number arises from a long chain of simple calculation steps. You could change each input a little, one at a time, and see what comes out at the end. With a million inputs, that would mean repeating the whole calculation a million times. Is there a faster way? And how do you check whether a formula for these sensitivities that you derived or programmed yourself is really correct? The payoff with the answers, you know which adjustable knobs a result depends on most strongly and how small measurement errors in the inputs affect the result. You can replace a complicated function near a point by a much simpler one and estimate how large the error is. And you can compute the sensitivities even when the number arises from a very long calculation with very many inputs. Almost every method that learns from data needs these tools. How to work with this chapter. The sections build on each other, and every new term has its own subsection with an example. Expandable boxes contain background why a method works and where it comes from , derivations and proofs; you do not need them to read on. Such a line through two points of a curve is called a secant line . Its slope is the difference in height between the two points divided by their horizontal distance. text: Many functions arise by substituting one function into another. text: A computer evaluates long formulas step by step, and each step is a simple operation with a known derivative. A computational graph makes these steps and their dependencies visible. This section draws such a graph, evaluates it forward as a table and writes its local derivative on each edge. With that, everything is prepared to compute the derivatives of the result with respect to all inputs mechanically. Intermediate results With the rules from Section 1.4 die ableitung.html stufe 1 4 , you can differentiate any formula that consists of basic arithmetic operations and known functions. If you write out the result as a formula, however, it often becomes much longer than the function itself. By the product rule, a product of factors has a derivative consisting of terms with factors each; so the formula grows with , while the function has only factors. With intermediate results, by contrast, the calculation stays small. After each step, you keep the current value and the current derivative and continue calculating with numbers, not with formulas. Let ; we are looking for . The written out product rule gives four terms, in each of which one factor is replaced by its derivative Fig. 17 abb 17 . Step by step, with the partial products , and the product rule , it goes like this Each step costs two multiplications and one addition, no matter how many factors have already been processed. The written out product rule for at the point in term , the factor is replaced by its derivative . ⁠ In short Written out derivative formulas quickly become much longer than the function; with intermediate results stored as numbers, the cost per step stays small. The computational graph Which intermediate results a calculation has and what each of them depends on is shown most clearly by a picture made of nodes and arrows. An arrow from a node to a node means is needed to compute . A computational graph consists of nodes and directed edges, that is, arrows between nodes. Each node stands for a number or, in larger calculations, for a whole vector or a matrix. The input nodes are the inputs of the calculation; every other node arises by an elementary operation from the nodes from which an edge leads to . These are called the predecessors of , and is called their successor. If you follow the edges, you never return to a node you have already visited; such a graph is called acyclic. One distinguished node is the result. Elementary operations are the basic arithmetic operations and functions of one variable such as the square, the exponential function or the logistic function. Because the graph is acyclic, you can always arrange the nodes so that each node comes after its predecessors; you calculate in this order. A program with loops and branches also yields such a graph for specific input values a loop that runs three times produces the same nodes three times in a row. The example of this section and the next is with the intermediate results and and the result . The graph has three input nodes, two addition nodes and one multiplication node, connected by six edges Fig. 18 abb 18 . The input has two successors; the graph branches there. The computational graph of . The arrows point in the direction of calculation; the circles contain the elementary operation. The values of the forward evaluation at the point are shown in green. ⁠ In short A computational graph breaks a calculation down into elementary operations; its edges show which value enters which other one, and because it is acyclic, there is always an order in which you can evaluate it. The forward evaluation Evaluating a computational graph means computing the nodes in an order in which each node comes after its predecessors. If you write the steps one below the other, you get a table that you also need for the derivatives all values are stored, not just the result. The forward evaluation of a computational graph computes all nodes in an order in which each node comes after its predecessors, and it stores every value. How strongly the successor responds to a small change in this one predecessor is an ordinary partial derivative of the elementary operation. For an edge from to , the partial derivative of the elementary operation that computes , taken with respect to its input , is called the local derivative of the edge. this is called symbolic differentiation, and by section 9.1 rechengraphen.html stufe 9 1 the formulas grow quickly in the process. you can evaluate the function at two nearby points and form a difference quotient; this is called numerical differentiation, it is only approximately correct, and section 11 numerische ableitung und gradientenprufung.html stufe 11 examines its error. the third way combines the advantages of the other two. automatic differentiation computes derivatives of a calculation by applying the chain rule to its computational graph it evaluates the local derivatives with the numbers of the calculation and combines them according to the sum over the paths. automatic differentiation calculates with numbers, not with formulas, and therefore no expressions swell. it approximates nothing the result is the exact derivative, distorted only by the rounding of the individual calculation steps. and it works for every program that consists of elementary operations, even with loops and branches, because for the given inputs the program yields a computational graph. the step by step calculation in the example in section 9.1 rechengraphen.html stufe 9 1 was already automatic differentiation. for 9.1 rechengraphen.html gl 9 1 , the previous section assembled the derivatives , and from the local derivatives, without multiplying out or differentiating the formula of . that was automatic differentiation, though still without a fixed procedure for the order of the calculation. the two following subsections give this order. ⁠ in short automatic differentiation applies the chain rule with numbers to the computational graph; it is exact up to rounding and needs no formula. forward mode the first option follows the calculation itself. you decide in which direction you change the inputs, and at each node you carry along, next to its value, how fast that value changes under this variation. in forward mode , you choose a direction for the inputs and compute, for each node , in addition to its value, the number in the same order as the values. this number is called the tangent value of ; the input nodes receive the components of as their tangent values. the name recalls the tangent line from section 1.2 die ableitung.html stufe 1 2 , but it is a number the tangent value is the rate of change of the node when you shift the inputs along the line . the formula 10.1 gl 10 1 is the chain rule along this curve, 6.4 die kettenregel fur mehrere variablen.html gl 6 4 , for a single node. after one pass, the result node holds . if the calculation has several outputs, they hold the product of the jacobian matrix with the direction. with , one pass yields the partial derivative with respect to , and with several outputs, column of the jacobian matrix. for the whole gradient of a function of variables, forward mode therefore needs passes. for 9.1 rechengraphen.html gl 9 1 at the point with the direction , this gives table 5 tab 5 . the result node holds . for and you need two more passes with and . table 5 forward mode for at the point in the direction . | node | computation | value | tangent value | | | | | | | | | | input | | | | | | input | | | | | | input | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | ⁠ in short forward mode carries a tangent value along with every value; one pass yields the derivative in one direction, that is, one column of the jacobian matrix. forward mode can be viewed as calculating with extended numbers. you calculate with pairs , where is a new symbol with the single rule ; such numbers are called dual numbers. addition and multiplication work as usual and , because the term drops out. so the factor in front of follows exactly the sum rule and the product rule. for 9.1 rechengraphen.html gl 9 1 , you set , , and get value and derivative with respect to in one calculation. for a function of one variable, you set , which corresponds to the linear approximation, in which the square of the small term plays no role. dual numbers were introduced by william kingdon clifford in 1873, long before any computer. reverse mode forward mode asks, for one input, how strongly each node depends on it. reverse mode asks the opposite question how strongly does the result depend on each node? this question can be answered backward, starting from the result, and at the end you know the answer for all inputs at once. the adjoint of a node is , the derivative of the result with respect to this node when you regard it as an input of the rest of the calculation. in reverse mode , you first carry out the forward evaluation and store all values. then you set and compute the nodes in reverse order, the adjoints of the input nodes form the gradient . the reverse order is necessary because each node needs the adjoints of its successors, and those come after it in the calculation. each adjoint has the same shape as its node; there, every method costs many passes. reverse mode has a price memory. the backward pass needs all values of the forward evaluation, because the local derivatives are evaluated with them. so you have to keep every intermediate value until the backward pass has gone past it. in long calculations, this memory is often the actual limit. let a function have inputs, and let one evaluation take one second. forward mode needs passes for the gradient, that is, at least seconds, just over days. central difference quotients need evaluations, just over days, and are then only approximately correct. reverse mode needs one forward evaluation and one backward pass, so with a few seconds. ⁠ in short reverse mode delivers all partial derivatives of a number for a small fixed multiple of one evaluation, independent of ; text: With the computational graph, derivatives can be computed mechanically, without rearranging formulas and exactly up to the rounding of the elementary operations. This is called automatic differentiation. There are two ways to combine the local derivatives forward, in step with the calculation, or backward, from the result to the inputs. Reverse mode delivers the derivative of a number with respect to all its inputs in a single pass, and this section shows why that costs so little. What automatic differentiation is There are three ways to get the derivative of a calculation. You can transform the formula with the rules; this is called symbolic differentiation, and by Section 9.1 rechengraphen.html stufe 9 1 the formulas grow quickly in the process. You can evaluate the function at two nearby points and form a difference quotient; this is called numerical differentiation, it is only approximately correct, and Section 11 numerische ableitung und gradientenprufung.html stufe 11 examines its error. The third way combines the advantages of the other two. Automatic differentiation computes derivatives of a calculation by applying the chain rule to its computational graph it evaluates the local derivatives with the numbers of the calculation and combines them according to the sum over the paths. Automatic differentiation calculates with numbers, not with formulas, and therefore no expressions swell. It approximates nothing the result is the exact derivative, distorted only by the rounding of the individual calculation steps. And it works for every program that consists of elementary operations, even with loops and branches, because for the given inputs the program yields a computational graph. The step by step calculation in the example in Section 9.1 rechengraphen.html stufe 9 1 was already automatic differentiation. For 9.1 rechengraphen.html gl 9 1 , the previous section assembled the derivatives , and from the local derivatives, without multiplying out or differentiating the formula of . That was automatic differentiation, though still without a fixed procedure for the order of the calculation. The two following subsections give this order. ⁠ In short Automatic differentiation applies the chain rule with numbers to the computational graph; it is exact up to rounding and needs no formula. Forward mode The first option follows the calculation itself. You decide in which direction you change the inputs, and at each node you carry along, next to its value, how fast that value changes under this variation. In forward mode , you choose a direction for the inputs and compute, for each node , in addition to its value, the number in the same order as the values. This number is called the tangent value of ; the input nodes receive the components of as their tangent values. The name recalls the tangent line from Section 1.2 die ableitung.html stufe 1 2 , but it is a number the tangent value is the rate of change of the node when you shift the inputs along the line . The formula 10.1 gl 10 1 is the chain rule along this curve, 6.4 die kettenregel fur mehrere variablen.html gl 6 4 , for a single node. After one pass, the result node holds . If the calculation has several outputs, they hold the product of the Jacobian matrix with the direction. With , one pass yields the partial derivative with respect to , and with several outputs, column of the Jacobian matrix. For the whole gradient of a function of variables, forward mode therefore needs passes. For 9.1 rechengraphen.html gl 9 1 at the point with the direction , this gives Table 5 tab 5 . The result node holds . For and you need two more passes with and . Forward mode can be viewed as calculating with extended numbers. You calculate with pairs , where is a new symbol with the single rule ; such numbers are called dual numbers. Addition and multiplication work as usual and , because the term drops out. So the factor in front of follows exactly the sum rule and the product rule. For 9.1 rechengraphen.html gl 9 1 , you set , , and get value and derivative with respect to in one calculation. For a function of one variable, you set , which corresponds to the linear approximation, in which the square of the small term plays no role. Dual numbers were introduced by William Kingdon Clifford in 1873, long before any computer. Reverse mode Forward mode asks, for one input, how strongly each node depends on it. Reverse mode asks the opposite question how strongly does the result depend on each node? This question can be answered backward, starting from the result, and at the end you know the answer for all inputs at once. The adjoint of a node is , the derivative of the result with respect to this node when you regard it as an input of the rest of the calculation. In reverse mode , you first carry out the forward evaluation and store all values. Then you set and compute the nodes in reverse order, The adjoints of the input nodes form the gradient . The reverse order is necessary because each node needs the adjoints of its successors, and those come after it in the calculation. Each adjoint has the same shape as its node; if a node is a vector or a matrix, its adjoint is also a vector or a matrix, as with the backward rule of the matrix product in Section 7.6 ableiten nach vektoren und matrizen.html stufe 7 6 . For every node , the number computed by 10.2 gl 10 2 is the sum over all paths from to the result, with the product of the local derivatives taken along each path. For the input nodes, by Section 9.4 rechengraphen.html stufe 9 4 , this is the partial derivative of . Group all paths from to the result by their first edge. Each path begins with an edge to a successor and then continues as a path from to the result. The paths that go via therefore contribute, together, times the sum over all paths from to the result. If this sum has already been computed correctly for all successors, that is, if it equals , then the sum for is exactly 10.2 gl 10 2 . For the result itself, the statement holds with , the empty path. Because you calculate backward, the successors always come before , and the statement carries over node by node all the way to the inputs. In the backward calculation, each adjoint travels against the direction of the arrows and is multiplied by the local derivative of the edge, and where two edges leave a node, as at , the contributions are added. ⁠ In short Reverse mode first calculates forward and stores all values, then calculates the adjoints backward; one backward pass yields the whole gradient. If you know these patterns, you can write down adjoints almost without calculation and quickly spot mistakes in derivations. An addition passes its adjoint on unchanged to each input. A multiplication passes on to each input its adjoint times the value of the other input. A maximum passes its adjoint on entirely to the larger input; the smaller one receives . Large differences in the orders of magnitude of the inputs therefore lead to equally large differences in the partial derivatives. The cost Why is reverse mode so important? Because it delivers the gradient of a function with very many inputs almost as cheaply as the function value itself. A comparison of the methods makes this clear. Forward mode needs passes for the gradient of a function of variables, one per input direction. One pass costs a small multiple of one evaluation of , because each elementary operation is accompanied by its tangent value. Difference quotients even need or evaluations. Reverse mode, by contrast, always needs exactly one forward evaluation and one backward pass, no matter how large is. In the backward pass, each edge is used exactly once, with one multiplication and one addition. So it, too, costs only a small multiple of the forward evaluation. Let be given by a computational graph of elementary operations, and let one evaluation cost the time . Then the whole Jacobian matrix costs about in forward mode and about in reverse mode. The number does not depend on and . If you count each basic arithmetic operation as one step, one can show that function value and gradient together need at most four times as many steps as the function value alone; if you also count the memory accesses, stays below , and in practice it is often between and . For a number , the whole gradient in reverse mode therefore costs only a fixed small multiple of one evaluation. The theorem is proved by counting, for each elementary operation, how many calculation steps its backward step needs relative to the operation itself. A rule of thumb follows many inputs and one output, as with a number that depends on millions of adjustable knobs, call for reverse mode. Few inputs and many outputs call for forward mode. For the complete Jacobian matrix of a function with many inputs and many outputs, there is no such trick; there, every method costs many passes. Reverse mode has a price memory. The backward pass needs all values of the forward evaluation, because the local derivatives are evaluated with them. So you have to keep every intermediate value until the backward pass has gone past it. In long calculations, this memory is often the actual limit. Let a function have inputs, and let one evaluation take one second. Forward mode needs passes for the gradient, that is, at least seconds, just over days. Central difference quotients need evaluations, just over days, and are then only approximately correct. Reverse mode needs one forward evaluation and one backward pass, so with a few seconds. ⁠ In short Reverse mode delivers all partial derivatives of a number for a small fixed multiple of one evaluation, independent of ; it pays for this with the memory for all intermediate values. The sum over all paths can have very many terms. If you chain ten calculation steps, each of which uses its predecessor twice, for example , there are paths between input and result, and with steps more than . Reverse mode never counts these paths individually. It combines all paths that go through the same node in that node's adjoint and reuses this partial sum for all predecessors. This is the same idea as with the step by step product rule in Section 9.1 rechengraphen.html stufe 9 1 an intermediate result is computed once and then used often. So each edge costs one multiplication and one addition, and the cost grows with the number of edges, not with the number of paths. The memory requirement can be reduced by keeping only some intermediate values and recomputing the others during the backward pass; with a clever distribution, the memory and the factor by which the computing time exceeds that of a plain evaluation then grow only logarithmically with the length of the calculation. Forward mode was described as a computer program in 1964. Seppo Linnainmaa developed reverse mode in 1970 in his master's thesis at the University of Helsinki, in order to estimate how the rounding errors of all calculation steps affect the result; the sensitivity of the result to each intermediate step is exactly that step's adjoint. A program that automatically generated reverse mode for arbitrary calculations followed in 1980. text: You can also estimate derivatives without a formula you evaluate the function at two nearby points and form the difference quotient. This is too slow for computing all derivatives of a function with many inputs, but ideal for checking a derivative that you derived or programmed. The gradient check If you derive a gradient by hand or program it as backward steps, it is easy to make mistakes a forgotten path, a missing transpose, a wrong factor. A difference quotient needs no derivation; it only evaluates the function. Comparing the two finds such mistakes reliably. The linear approximation of a number tells how it responds to small changes in its inputs each input contributes its partial derivative times its change, and the contributions add up to the dot product with the gradient. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, for steps of fixed length this dot product is largest in the direction of the gradient, which therefore points uphill most steeply and is perpendicular to the contour lines. If the number arises from a long chain of calculation steps, its derivative is a product of Jacobian matrices, that is, a sum over all paths, and reverse mode computes this product starting from the number with row vectors, so that it delivers all derivatives at once for a small multiple of the cost of a single evaluation. One principle behind all the results. Almost everything in this chapter follows from one principle close enough to a point, every differentiable function is linear.
